## **Selectional Restrictions and Order**
<br>
.pull-left[
the **selectional restrictions** of affixes often help us **determine** the order in which
they were attached<br><br>
- consider the following polymorphemic word<br><br>
  - <i>**re**-<b>play-<span style="color:green">able</span></b></i><br><br>
- which affix was attached **first** to the root *<b>play</b>*?
]
.pull-right[<img src="../pic/0921/morphosyn.jpg" width="65%">]<br><br><br><br>

--

- ***re-*** has to be attached first, since it cannot attach to adjectives <br><br>
  - *<b>play</b>* → <i>**re**-<b>play</b></i> → <i>**re**-<b>play-<span style="color:green">able</span></b></i>


---
## **Morphological Tree Drawing**
### **De-humid-ify-er**
<br>
1. identify the word's morphemes and write them out separately in one row
2. identify the root (or roots) and label its **part of speech**
3. look at the morphemes immediately before and after the root<br>
  check **which one is added first**, draw lines upward connecting them, <br>
  and **label** the new words's part of speech
4. this new word becomes the base you'll keep building off of<br>
  **repeat step 3** using this new base<br><br>

--

## **Morphological Structure: Ambiguity**
<br><br>
.pull-left[
<br><br><br>
.pull-left[
*un* + *able*<br><br>
<img src="../pic/0921/undo3.png" width="90%">
]
.pull-right[
*undo* + *able*<br><br>
<img src="../pic/0921/undo4.png" width="90%">
]
]
.pull-right[
- the case of **unlockable** is an example of a word with an **ambiguous structure**<br><br>
- depending on the structure you assign it, it has a **different meaning**<br><br>
- both meanings are acceptable <br><br>
- which means the **meaning** of words is directly affected by their morphological structure<br><br>
- that's why **structure** is important, without knowing the structure, we would not be able to be **compositional** properly
]

## **Morphological Process I: Affixation**
<br>
.pull-left[
- **affixation**: adding an affix (a prefix, suffix, infix, or circumfix)<br><br>
  - depending on the type of affix, also called <span style="color:green"><b>prefixation</b></span>, <span style="color:blue"><b>suffixation</b></span>, **infixation**, <span style="color:orange"><b>circumfixation</b></span><br><br>
  - <span style="color:green"><b>prefixation</b></span><br>
  *<span style="color:green"><b>re-</b></span> + visit → revisit*<br>
  - <span style="color:blue"><b>suffixation</b></span><br>
  *modern + <span style="color:blue"><b>-ize</b></span>* → *modernize*<br>
  - **infixation**<br>
  (Tagalog) *bili* 'buy' → *b**-um-**ili* 'to buy'<br>
  - <span style="color:orange"><b>circumfixation</b></span><br>
  (Indonesian) *ajar* 'teach' → *<span style="color:orange"><b>pel</b></span>-ajar-<span style="color:orange"><b>an</b></span>* 'subject'
]
.pull-right[
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/0921/suffix.jpg" width="90%">]

---
## **Morphological Process II: Compounding**
<br>
.pull-left[
- **compounding**: combining **two or more roots** into a single word<br><br>
  - *tree + house → treehouse*
  - *blue + bird → bluebird*
  - *snow + white → Snowwhite*<br><br>
- compound words usually contains more specific meaning than two separate words<br><br>
- compound words often sound different from the words used separately – <u>one of the roots will be pronounced with **less stress**</u> than if it had been a separate word:<br><br>
  - *Abraham Lincoln was born in a log cabin – a <span style="color:green"><b>tree house</b></span>*.
  - *The child played in a <span style="color:orange"><b>treehouse</b></span>*.
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0921/treehouse1.png" width="50%"><br><br>
<img src="../pic/0921/treehouse2.png" width="70%">
</div>
]

## **Morphological Process II: Compounding**
<br>
.pull-left[
- **compounding**: combining **two or more roots** into a single word<br><br>
- different languages have different rules for compounding<br><br>
- **Germanic languages** are well-known for <u>permitting lots of compounding</u><br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0921/german.png" width="100%">
</div><br>
- **English** is also a Germanic language and allows this kind of compounding<br><br>
- the meaning of compounds is usually **non-compositional**
]
.pull-right[
<br><br><img src="../pic/0921/literal.jpg" width="100%">
]

## **Morphological Process III: Reduplication**
<br>
.pull-left[
- **reduplication**: repeating all or part of a morpheme<br><br>
- <span style="color:green"><b>English</b></span> examples:<br><br>
  - *Do you just like him as a friend, or do you <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>like-like</b></span> him*?<br><br>
  - *Yesterday, we just went out for coffee, but this weekend we're going on a <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>date-date</b></span>*.<br><br>
  - *Whenever we go to a <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>fancy-shmancy</b></span> restaurant, we feel like James Bond*.<br><br>
  - *He's just a baby! <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>Baby-shmaby</b></span>, he's five years old*!
]
.pull-right[
<br><br><img src="../pic/0921/wugwug.png" width="70%">
]


---
## **Morphological Process III: Reduplication**
<br>
.pull-left[
<br>
<img src="../pic/0921/diction.jpg" width="100%">
]
.pull-right[
- **reduplication** is more productive in some other languages, serves an explicit **grammatical** purpose:<br><br>

**full reduplication**: repeat **ALL** of a morpheme
- <span style="color:orange"><b>Indonesian</b></span> plural
  - *orang* 'person' $\rightarrow$ *orang*-*orang* 'people'
- <span style="color:green"><b>Chinese</b></span> intensified adjective:
  - <em>kʰai<sup>55</sup>ʂin<sup>55</sup></em> 'happy' $\rightarrow$ <em>kʰai<sup>55</sup>kʰai<sup>55</sup> ʂin<sup>55</sup>ʂin<sup>55</sup></em> 'very happy'
<br><br>

**partial reduplication**: repeat **PART** of a morpheme
- <span style="color:blue"><b>Tagalog</b></span> future
  - *bili* 'buy' $\rightarrow$ *<b>bi</b>-bili* 'will buy'
- <span style="color:brown"><b>Kazakh</b></span> intensified adjective:
  - *tætti* 'sweet' $\rightarrow$ *<b>tæp</b>-tætti* 'very sweet'
]


---
## **Morphological Process IV: Alternation**
<br>
.pull-left[
- **alternation**: changing one or more sounds within the morpheme<br><br>
- usually <u>most of the sounds stay the same</u>, but one or a few are changed
- alternation can result in *irregular* nouns, verbs, etc.<br>
- what is the difference in **sound** in these words and what is the difference in **meaning**? (inflection or derivation?)<br><br>
  - <i>goose</i>, <i>g**ee**se</i>
  - <i>r**i**ng</i>, <i>r**a**ng</i>, <i>r**u**ng</i>
  - <i>Does the baby have tee**th** yet? No, she hasn't yet started to tee**the**</i>.
  - this tool has no u**se**. What are you talking about – I u**se** it every day</i>.
]
.pull-right[<br><br><img src="../pic/0921/geese.jpg" width="100%">]

---
## **Morphological Process V: Suppletion**
<br>
.pull-left[<br><img src="../pic/0921/goodest.jpg" width="100%">]
.pull-right[
- **suppletion**: when an inflected form is **phonetically very different** from other forms of the same word (the result is even more highly irregular)<br><br>
- **English** examples:<br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">PAST TENSE</div>
  - **regular**: *walk → walked*, *jump → jumped*<br>
  - <span style="color:green"><b>suppletive</b></span>: *is → was*, *go → went*<br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">COMPARATIVE / SUPERLATIVE</div>
  - **regular**: *nice → nicer → nicest*<br>
  <span style="color:white"><b>regular</b>:</span> *big → bigger → biggest*<br>
  - <span style="color:green"><b>suppletive</b></span>: *good → better → best*<br>
  <span style="color:white"><b>suppletive</b>:</span> *bad → worse → worst*
]


---

## **Multiple Processes**
<br><br><br>
### some words exhibit **multiple morphological processes**
<br><br>
### *break* → *broke* (alternation)<br>
### *break* → *brok(e)-en* (alternation + suffixing)

<br>

<br><br>
how is Calvin (the child) using language in a creative or unusual way?<br>
is Hobbes (the tiger) correct that Calvin's phrasing is a "complete impediment to understanding"?

---
## **Morphological Process VI: Zero Derivation**
<br>
.pull-left[
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/0921/derivation.jpg" width="100%">
]
.pull-right[
- we know that **derivational** morphemes can change a word's part of speech:
  - *magnet* (N) → *magnet-ize* (V)
  - *atom* (N) → *atom-ic* (Adj)<br><br>
- English can sometimes change a word's **part of speech** without adding anything
  - *I'm going to <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>jump</b></span> (V) over that railing*.
  - *That was a nice <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>jump</b></span> (N)*!<br><br>
  - *Please send me an <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>email</b></span> (N) about that*.
  - *OK, I <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>emailed</b></span> (V) you*!<br><br>
- **zero-derivation**: deriving a new word with a **different part of speech** by adding nothing <br><br>
- not all languages can do this! how about yours?
]

## **Morphological Types of Languages**
<br>
languages can be classified according to the way they **use** or **don’t use** <u>morphological processes</u><br><br>

--

.pull-left[
**analytic/isolating language**<br><br>
- made up of sequences of **free morphemes**
- NO <span style="color:green"><b>affixes</b></span> are used to compose words
- <span style="color:blue"><b>Mandarin Chinese</b></span>
  - the past tense is expressed with a functional free morpheme (tones omitted):

    <td style="text-align:left;">tæ<sup>35</sup>n</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">tɕi<sup>35</sup>n]</td>
    <td style="text-align:left; color:white">lə</td>
  </tr>

    </td>

    <td style="text-align:left;">[wɔ<sup>214</sup></td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">mə<sup>35</sup>n</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">tæ<sup>35</sup>n</td>

    <td style="text-align:left;">lə</td>
  </tr>

## **Morphological Types of Languages**
<br>
languages can be classified according to the way they **use** or **don’t use** <u>morphological processes</u><br><br>

--
**synthetic language**<br><br>
- **bound morphemes** can be attached to other morphemes
- so a word can be made of <span style="color:green"><b>several types</b></span> of meaningful elements 
- yet there are different ways to put together morphemes, resulting in different types of synthetic languages:
___

--

.pull-left[
A. **agglutinating**: the morphemes are joined together loosely, it is easy to determine the boundaries between morphemes
  - one morpheme has **only one** meaning<br>
  - <span style="color:blue"><b>Japanese</b></span>, Turkish, etc.
<br><br>
<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse;">
  <tr>
    <td style="text-align:left;">piano</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">o</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">hiki</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">-ma</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">-shi</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">-ta</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td style="text-align:left;">piano</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">ACC</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">play</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">POL</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">POL</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">PST</td>
    <td></td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td colspan="6" style="text-align:left; padding-bottom:20px;">
    'We played the piano.'
    </td>
  </tr>
</table>
]

--

.pull-right[
B. **fusional**: morphemes are “fused” with
the stem and can be hard to tell where the boundary is
  - a single affix can convey **several** meanings simultaneously and there can be **alternations** to
the forms of both the stems and affixes
  - <span style="color:blue"><b>Greek</b></span>, Spanish, etc.
<br><br>
<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse;">
  <tr>
    <td style="text-align:left;">pez</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">-a</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">-me</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">to</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">piano</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td style="text-align:left;">play</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">TH</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">1PL.PST</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">the</td>
    <td style="text-align:left;">piano</td>
    <td></td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td colspan="5" style="text-align:left; padding-bottom:20px;">
    'We were playing the piano.'
    </td>
  </tr>
</table>
]
